input.question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?
input.ground_truth: Because over a given part of the earth the wind moves predominantly in one direction . Hence one way the plane is flying into the wind and one it's flying with the wind. At the altitude of airliners the wind speeds constitute a noticeable fraction of the nominal speed of the aircraft - hence the difference. EDIT: I should have added that for this reason I wouldn't expect to see the affect you're describing on a generally north-south routing (eg london - cape town).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why a flight going East to West takes longer than exact same flight going West to East?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine Earth is like a big, round ball that spins around. When you fly east (the same way the Earth spins), the Earth is also moving under you, kind of like running on a moving walkway at the airport. This can make your trip a little longer because you’re “chasing” the ground that’s moving away from you.

But if you fly west (against the way the Earth spins), the Earth is kind of helping you by moving towards you, like walking against a moving walkway. This can make your trip a little shorter.

So, sometimes a flight going east takes a bit longer than the same flight going west, because of how the Earth spins!
